heroLead: Dry Tavern is a small rural community in Greene County, ground that sits well within one of the most consistently drilled corners of the entire Marcellus play.
intro: Greene County has drawn operator interest for both Marcellus and deeper Utica development for well over a decade, and Dry Tavern-area farmland sits squarely within that footprint. For families here, that often means an active lease, a real production history, and royalty statements that reflect genuine drilling activity rather than a dormant lease sitting untouched.

We buy Dry Tavern-area mineral and royalty interests directly, and because this county has such an established drilling record, we're often able to point to specific nearby activity when evaluating what your interest is worth.

sections.heading: Ground in the Play
paragraphs: This part of Greene County ranks among the most active in the state, with operators like CNX and EQT holding substantial acreage positions and a long track record of drilling. That established history means we can often reference actual nearby well performance rather than relying on general regional trends, which gives owners a clearer, more grounded sense of what's driving any offer we make.
It also means title work here tends to be more thoroughly documented than in less-developed counties, since so many transactions have already run through the process before.

sections.heading: Rural Land, Real Production History
paragraphs: Dry Tavern's rural character has meant large contiguous tracts have been common building blocks for drilling units here, and families with sizable farm or timber acreage often find their land is part of an established, producing unit rather than an unleased or speculative one. If your family has been receiving royalty checks tied to a Dry Tavern-area unit for years, we can review that production history as part of making you an offer.

sections.heading: What Deep-Core Activity Means for Deductions
paragraphs: Established, heavily developed acreage like this can still carry meaningful post-production cost deductions on the royalty statement, gathering and compression infrastructure has to be paid for somewhere, and Pennsylvania law generally allows those costs to be deducted unless a specific lease prohibits it. We'll look at your actual statement and tell you honestly whether what you're seeing looks typical for this area.

faqs.question: Is Dry Tavern in an actively producing part of Greene County?
faqs.answer: Yes, this is one of the more consistently drilled parts of the state, though we still check the specific activity tied to your particular tract.

faqs.question: Does more drilling history make the title work easier?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. Areas with a long transaction history tend to have more thoroughly documented title, though we still verify everything carefully.

faqs.question: Why do I still see deductions on my check from an established, producing well?
faqs.answer: Post-production costs like gathering and compression are typically legal deductions unless your specific lease prohibits them, even on well-established production.
